questions.stem: What is a magnetic field line?

options.text: a line showing the direction of the force on a north pole
options.explanation: The field-line direction is defined by the north-pole force.

options.text: a line showing the path iron filings melt along
options.explanation: Filings align with the field; nothing melts.

options.text: the track a magnet slides along
options.explanation: Field lines map force direction, not motion tracks.

options.text: the outline of the magnet itself
options.explanation: The field exists in the space around the magnet, beyond its outline.

questions.stem: Outside a bar magnet, field lines run:

options.text: in circles around the middle of the magnet
options.explanation: Circles belong to current-carrying wires, not bar magnets.

options.text: out of the north pole and into the south pole
options.explanation: The external flow is north to south by convention.

options.text: from the south pole to the north pole
options.explanation: That reverses the direction convention.

options.text: straight out of both poles without return
options.explanation: Field lines are continuous loops, not open rays.

questions.stem: Two field line diagrams of the same magnet are drawn. In diagram A the lines near a pole are crowded; in diagram B they are spread out. Compare the field strengths.

options.text: both show equal strength
options.explanation: Line spacing is the strength cue; different spacing means different strength.

options.text: neither diagram encodes strength
options.explanation: Density is exactly how strength is encoded.

options.text: A shows the stronger field there
options.explanation: Crowded lines mean stronger field at that place.

options.text: B shows the stronger field there
options.explanation: Spaced-out lines indicate a weaker field.

questions.stem: Why can two magnetic field lines never cross?

options.text: crossing lines would make the magnet too heavy
options.explanation: Field lines are drawings, not physical objects.

options.text: they can cross, but only at the poles
options.explanation: Even at poles the field has one local direction.

options.text: crossing would reverse the compass direction
options.explanation: The impossibility is the two-direction reading, not compass damage.

options.text: the field has one direction at each point, and a crossing would give two
options.explanation: A single-valued field forbids intersecting lines.

questions.stem: A plotting compass is placed at a point near a bar magnet. What does its needle show?

options.text: the needle's north end points along the field line there
options.explanation: The compass north is a north pole pushed along the field direction.

options.text: the needle always points to geographic north
options.explanation: Near a magnet the local field can overpower Earth's field.

options.text: the needle points at the magnet's middle
options.explanation: It aligns with the local field line, not the magnet's centre.

options.text: the needle spins continuously
options.explanation: A steady field gives a steady alignment.

questions.modelAnswer: A line whose direction at any point is the direction of the magnetic force on a north pole placed there.

questions.stem: State what the spacing of field lines tells you about the field.
questions.modelAnswer: Closer spacing of field lines means a stronger magnetic field at that point.

questions.stem: Explain how iron filings reveal the field pattern around a bar magnet.
questions.modelAnswer: Each filing becomes an induced magnet in the field and turns to lie along the local field-line direction. Across the whole sheet the filings therefore line up end-to-end in curves, tracing the pattern from the north pole round to the south pole and bunching where the field is strongest.

questions.stem: A student maps a bar magnet's field with a plotting compass: marking the needle direction at each point and stepping the compass along. Describe the map that builds up.
questions.modelAnswer: The marked steps chain into smooth curves leaving the magnet's north pole and entering the south pole. The curves are closest together at the poles, showing the strongest field there, and they never cross anywhere on the map.

questions.stem: What is a uniform magnetic field?

options.text: one that changes direction every few millimetres
options.explanation: That is the opposite of uniform.

options.text: one with the same strength and direction at every point
options.explanation: Uniformity fixes both magnitude and direction.

options.text: one with lines of different lengths
options.explanation: Line length carries no meaning here; uniformity is even spacing.

options.text: one found only inside a magnet
options.explanation: Uniform fields are set up in the gap between poles.

questions.stem: How are the field lines drawn in a uniform field?

options.text: crossing at regular intervals
options.explanation: Field lines never cross, uniform or not.

options.text: radiating from a single point
options.explanation: Radial patterns belong to single poles, not uniform gaps.

options.text: straight, parallel and equally spaced
options.explanation: This is the drawn signature of uniformity.

options.text: curved and bunching at the edges
options.explanation: Curves and bunching mean the field varies — non-uniform.

questions.stem: Which arrangement produces a uniform field between the magnets?

options.text: two bar magnets with like poles facing
options.explanation: Like poles facing give a neutral point, not a uniform gap.

options.text: one magnet on its own
options.explanation: A single bar magnet's field is strongly non-uniform.

options.text: two magnets end to end in a line
options.explanation: End-to-end stacking strengthens poles; it does not open a uniform gap.

options.text: two bar magnets with opposite poles facing
options.explanation: North facing south sets up the even gap field.

questions.stem: A plotting compass is moved across the gap between two facing opposite poles. What does the needle do?

options.text: it points the same direction at every position in the gap
options.explanation: Uniform field means one constant direction throughout.

options.text: it reverses as it crosses the middle
options.explanation: Reversal happens at neutral points of like-pole gaps, not here.

options.text: it spins faster near the poles
options.explanation: A steady uniform field gives a steady alignment.

options.text: it points at whichever magnet is nearer
options.explanation: It aligns with the resultant uniform field, not the nearest magnet.

questions.stem: The gap between two facing poles is widened from 2 cm to 8 cm. What happens to the uniform region?

options.text: the magnets demagnetise
options.explanation: Gap width does not demagnetise permanent magnets.

options.text: a smaller fraction of the gap stays uniform
options.explanation: Fringing fields claim a proportionally larger share of a wide gap.

options.text: the whole wider gap becomes uniform
options.explanation: Widening adds fringing regions, not uniformity.

options.text: the field direction reverses
options.explanation: The north-to-south direction is unchanged by the gap size.

questions.stem: State how two permanent magnets are arranged to give a uniform field.
questions.modelAnswer: Place two bar magnets a short distance apart with opposite poles facing each other.

questions.stem: State the three drawing properties of a uniform field's field lines.
questions.modelAnswer: The lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced.

questions.stem: Explain why equally spaced parallel lines represent a field of constant strength.
questions.modelAnswer: Field strength is read from the density of field lines, so equal spacing everywhere means the same number of lines per unit area at every position. Parallel straightness adds that the direction never changes, so both the magnitude and the direction of the field are constant — the definition of a uniform field.

questions.stem: A school Hall-effect probe reads the field at five points across the gap between two facing opposite poles: the readings are equal. Which field property does this verify, and how would the readings behave near a single magnet instead?
questions.modelAnswer: Equal readings at all five points verify the field is uniform in the gap — same strength and direction everywhere. Near a single bar magnet the readings would rise sharply towards either pole and change direction around the magnet, because that field is non-uniform.
